opus-5.5.text:
Reliability is, I think, the whole ballgame for consumer agents, and it's the part that tends to get underestimated in the hype.

There's a real distinction between capability and reliability. Capability is whether a system *can* do something some of the time, and benchmarks and demos mostly measure that. Reliability is whether it does the right thing nearly every time, under messy real-world conditions. For a lot of consumer tasks, like booking a flight, ordering groceries, or managing your email, a system that works 90% of the time isn't 90% useful. It might be close to zero, or even negative, because you have to check its work every time. If I have to verify every booking, I might as well have done it myself.

Errors also compound. An agent task is a long chain of steps, and even if each step is pretty reliable, the chance of getting all of them right drops quickly. A small per-step failure rate becomes a large end-to-end failure rate. And the failures aren't always graceful. Ordering the wrong thing or sending an email to the wrong person has real costs, sometimes irreversible ones.

So I don't think the bottleneck for consumer agents is mainly about making models smarter. It's an engineering problem: designing systems that know when they're uncertain, ask for confirmation at the right moments, and make actions reversible where possible. That's less glamorous than a new frontier model, but it's what determines whether people actually use these things.

My expectation is that we'll see adoption first in narrower, lower-stakes domains where mistakes are cheap and easy to catch, and much slower progress on the "do everything for me" general assistant. That's not a knock on the technology. Diffusion of any technology goes through this phase of figuring out reliability, and it usually takes longer than the people building it expect.

r001.rationale: The response says reliability determines whether consumers use agents and predicts gradual adoption, but it does not suggest that reliably realizing existing capabilities could produce an economic transformation.

r002.rationale: It states that a system working 90% of the time for consumer tasks may be close to zero or even negative in usefulness because users must check its work, clearly conveying that 10% failure can make an agent unusable.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think reliability is really the whole ballgame for consumer agents right now, and it's a dimension that's been underappreciated relative to capability.

Here's the way I think about it. If you have an assistant that books a flight for you, and it gets it right ninety percent of the time, that sounds impressive on a benchmark. But from the consumer's perspective, a ten percent failure rate on something like booking a flight is unacceptable. You'd have to check its work every single time, and at that point you haven't saved any effort. You've actually added a layer of verification on top of the task you were trying to avoid doing. So the value of an agent doesn't scale linearly with accuracy. It's closer to a threshold. Below some level of reliability, the agent is worth roughly nothing to you, and above it, it becomes transformative.

And that threshold is higher than people assume, because of compounding. Agentic tasks are multi-step. If each step is ninety-five percent reliable and there are twenty steps, you're well below fifty percent for the overall task. So we've spent a lot of time on the capability frontier, on whether the model can do the task in principle, and much less on whether it does it consistently, every time, under the messy conditions of a real person's inbox or calendar or browser.

There's also a cost asymmetry that matters a lot in the consumer setting. The upside of an agent that works is convenience. The downside of an agent that fails is sometimes an irreversible action, like a purchase or a sent email or a deleted file. Those are not symmetric, and people are rightly risk-averse about handing over control when the failure modes are that costly. So I think the near-term path is agents that are scoped narrowly, that ask for confirmation at the right moments, and that are evaluated on reliability in the wild rather than on one-shot benchmark scores.

The optimistic version is that this is an engineering problem rather than a fundamental one. A lot of what makes agents unreliable today is about tooling, interfaces, and evaluation, not just about model intelligence. But I do think the field has to take it seriously as a first-class research problem rather than assuming it falls out of scaling.

r001.rationale: The response says reliability could make consumer agents “transformative,” but it does not communicate an economic transformation.

r002.rationale: It says a flight-booking agent with a 10% failure rate is unacceptable and would require checking every time, eliminating its usefulness.

astra-6.text:
I think reliability is going to be a central constraint. An agent can be very impressive in a demonstration, but as a consumer, you need to know whether you can trust it to complete your particular task. Those are different standards.

When you move from answering a question to taking actions, errors can have consequences. If an agent makes the wrong purchase or sends a message to the wrong person, you can’t necessarily fix that by generating another response. And if you have to watch every step, a lot of the benefit of delegation disappears. You’ve traded doing the task for supervising the agent.

So I’d look less at whether an agent can accomplish a task once and more at how consistently it succeeds, whether it recognizes when it needs help, and whether mistakes are easy to recover from. We don’t need perfect reliability for every use case. But we do need reliability that matches the stakes, and a way for consumers to understand where those limits are.

r001.rationale: The response says reliability constrains usefulness and delegation, but does not suggest that reliably realizing agents’ existing capabilities could produce an economic transformation.

r002.rationale: The response discusses consistency and stakes but gives no 10% failure rate or claim that this rate could make a consumer agent unusable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reliability is going to be a major constraint on how useful these agents are. There’s a big difference between a system that gives you a suggestion, which you can review, and one that takes actions on your behalf. If it books the wrong flight or sends a message to the wrong person, that’s a much harder error to recover from.

And with agents, you’re often talking about a sequence of steps. Even if each step is fairly reliable, that doesn’t mean the whole task will be. The question is whether the system can recognize when something has gone wrong, recover from it, or ask you for help.

For consumers, the practical test is how much supervision you need to provide. If you have to watch every action and check every result, you may end up doing as much work as you would have done yourself. So I expect usefulness to emerge task by task, especially where mistakes are easy to detect and undo, and where the agent actually saves you effort after you account for that oversight.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability as a constraint on usefulness and consumer effort, but does not suggest that realizing agents’ capabilities could produce an economic transformation.

r002.rationale: The response explains that errors can be costly and multi-step tasks can fail, but does not state that a consumer agent may be unusable with a 10% failure rate.
